संवाद न्यूज एजेंसी
फरीदाबाद। शहर में पिछले दिनों हुई बारिश से भले ही सुबह और शाम के मौसम में बदलाव आया हो, लेकिन दिन में तेज धूप और उमस ने लोगों की परेशानी बढ़ा दी है। सोमवार को जिले में अधिकतम तापमान 33 डिग्री सेल्सियस और न्यूनतम तापमान 26 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया। वातावरण में आर्द्रता 65 प्रतिशत रही।
आर्द्रता अधिक होने के कारण दिनभर लोग पसीने से परेशान रहे। उमस का असर इस कदर रहा कि घर या कार्यालय से थोड़ी देर के लिए बाहर निकलने पर ही लोगों के कपड़े पसीने से भीग गए। शरीर से अधिक मात्रा में पानी निकलने के कारण चक्कर और उल्टी जैसी परेशानी भी सामने आने लगी। सुबह से निकली तेज धूप ने भी लोगों को बेहाल किया। दिन में गर्मी और उमस के कारण बाजारों तथा खुले स्थानों पर लोगों को परेशानी का सामना करना पड़ा। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार 20 अगस्त तक जिले में बारिश होने की संभावना बनी हुई है। बारिश होने की स्थिति में तापमान में गिरावट आ सकती है। इससे लोगों को उमस और गर्मी से कुछ राहत मिलने की उम्मीद है।

title: मध्य वियतनाम में फैली भीषण गर्मी की लहर 19 अगस्त को समाप्त होने की संभावना है। - Vietnam.vn

full_text:
राष्ट्रीय मौसम विज्ञान और जल विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र के अनुसार, मध्य क्षेत्र में फैली भीषण गर्मी की लहर 19 अगस्त को समाप्त होने की संभावना है।
18 अगस्त को, क्वांग त्रि से दा नांग शहर तक का क्षेत्र, क्वांग न्गाई से डाक लक और खान्ह होआ प्रांतों के पूर्वी भाग में भीषण गर्मी पड़ी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में तो अत्यधिक गर्मी का प्रकोप रहा। अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा, कुछ स्थानों पर यह 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक था। न्यूनतम सापेक्ष आर्द्रता आमतौर पर 55-60% थी, और यह भीषण गर्मी सुबह 11 बजे से शाम 5 बजे तक बनी रही।
मौसम पूर्वानुमान विभाग के उप प्रमुख गुयेन हुउ थान्ह ने बताया, "हीटवे बुलेटिन में तापमान का पूर्वानुमान और बाहर का वास्तविक तापमान कंक्रीट या डामर जैसी सतहों की स्थिति के आधार पर 1-3 डिग्री या उससे भी अधिक भिन्न हो सकता है। हीटवेव के कारण प्राकृतिक आपदा का खतरा स्तर 1 है।"
17 अगस्त को उत्तरी वियतनाम के मध्य और निचले इलाकों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ी; थान्ह होआ से दा नांग शहर तक, क्वांग न्गाई से लेकर डाक लक और खान्ह होआ तक के प्रांतों के पूर्वी हिस्सों में भी भीषण गर्मी रही, कुछ क्षेत्रों में दोपहर 1 बजे तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहा, और कुछ स्थानों पर 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक रहा, जैसे: होई शुआन (थान्ह होआ) 37.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कोन कुओंग (न्घे आन) 37.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस, हा तिन्ह 37.3 डिग्री सेल्सियस, दा नांग 37.7 डिग्री सेल्सियस…; दोपहर 1 बजे सापेक्ष आर्द्रता आमतौर पर 55-60% के बीच रही।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
जलवायु पूर्वानुमान विभाग के उप प्रमुख गुयेन डुक होआ के अनुसार, अगस्त 2026 में, देश भर में औसत तापमान आम तौर पर कई वर्षों के औसत से 0.5-1 डिग्री सेल्सियस अधिक होगा, और कुछ क्षेत्रों में यह और भी अधिक हो सकता है।
दक्षिण मध्य तटीय क्षेत्र में गर्म मौसम जारी है और आने वाले दिनों में भी कई और गर्म दिन रहने की संभावना है, जिनकी संख्या पिछले कई वर्षों के औसत से अधिक हो सकती है। भीषण गर्मी को लेकर सावधानी बरतने की जरूरत है, क्योंकि कुछ क्षेत्रों में असाधारण रूप से भीषण गर्मी पड़ रही है। उत्तरी क्षेत्र और थान्ह होआ से ह्यू तक के प्रांतों और शहरों में, पिछले कई वर्षों के औसत की तुलना में गर्म मौसम में कमी आने की संभावना है।
जुलाई में, उत्तरी क्षेत्र में 12 से 14 जुलाई तक व्यापक लू चली, जिसमें अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 36-38 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहा और कुछ क्षेत्रों में 39 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक हो गया।
थान्ह होआ से लेकर ह्यू तक के क्षेत्र और दक्षिण मध्य तटीय क्षेत्र में 7-8 जुलाई, 14-23 जुलाई और 26-27 जुलाई को तीन लू चलीं, जिनमें दैनिक अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 36-39 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहा और कुछ स्थानों पर 40 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक हो गया।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
वियतनाम के मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी क्षेत्रों में कुछ दिनों तक स्थानीय स्तर पर लू चलने की संभावना है, जहां दैनिक अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच जाएगा।

title: Extreme Heat Is Hurting South Asia’s Economies. Here’s How Much. - The Diplomat – Asia

full_text:
Exposure to extreme heat is costing the South Asian workforce a significant chunk of their pay every year, a series of recently published reports show. The single largest economic cost of heat comes from labor productivity losses, but there are other factors as well. A report from the World Bank predicted that South Asia’s regional GDP could be reduced by nearly 7 percent by 2050 if no adaptation measures are taken.
A recent report from Bangladesh, which is based on interviews with 175 households engaged in informal work such as construction, rickshaw pulling, and garment manufacturing, found that outdoor workers lost about 8.5 percent of their annual income, as they lost roughly 24 working days a year. Indoor workers lost 14 working days and 4.5 percent of their annual income. For both groups, illness caused by heat and reduced productivity are the largest causes of workdays lost.
The report, titled “No escaping the heat: Health and economic impacts of heat stress on informal workers in urban Bangladesh,” estimates the nation is losing about 0.9 percent of its GDP due to workday losses. That figure further increases if the cost of kidney-related ailments due to frequent dehydration is taken into account. Workers reported low mood, mistakes at work, anxiety, and irritability, as well as difficulty sleeping.
The London-headquartered International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED) conducted the study jointly with the Dhaka-based Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP). The report comes close on the heels of two other publications that point to similar findings for the South Asian region.
A July 2026 report by IIED said India’s nationwide cost of heat-related kidney problems, combined with employees’ reduced ability to work during heatwaves, is estimated to be $78 billion in lost wages – equivalent to 1.99 percent of India’s GDP in 2024. Based on a survey conducted on 538 informal worker households in three Indian cities, Ajmer, Delhi, and Agra, the IIED study found a picture very similar to that of Bangladesh.
Those in outdoor industries like construction, road laying and brickmaking lost about 24 days of work annually due to heat, costing them the equivalent of $151 — nearly a tenth of their annual earnings. Indoor workers engaged in food packaging, garment manufacturing, and stonemasonry lost roughly 15 days — the equivalent of $89.
The overall loss of work hours translates to a massive scale of lost employment opportunities. Regarding South Asia, a World Bank report, titled “A Livable Future: Tackling Extreme Heat for Jobs and Growth in South Asia’s Cities,” published at the end of July, said that extreme heat “already subtracts the equivalent of 31 million full-time jobs a year across the region.”
The report examines how urban heat threatens the job market in Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, and Sri Lanka. It estimates that, on average, rising temperatures will lower labor productivity in South Asia by 11 percent below the baseline by 2050. This is the largest estimated loss for any emerging market and developing economy region.
As another 2026 report on South and Southeast Asian cities, titled “Hot Cities Make Hard Work Harder,” points out, even in a Himalayan city like Nepal’s Kathmandu, 85 percent of respondents reported wage losses and increased healthcare expenses due to extreme heat. In Delhi, they found workers risk being sent home without pay when the heat slows output and targets are missed.
Sri Lanka is not immune from heat stress either. A 2025 study reported that the island nation lost a total of $10.87 billion in 2023 due to reduced work hours.
According to Ritu Bharadwaj, IIED’s director of climate resilience, finance, and loss and damage, for these workers, heat exposure doesn’t end when their shift ends. “They leave a hot worksite for a home with a tin roof, one fan, and frequent power cuts, giving no chance to recover,” she said.
Across South Asia, many informal workers in megacities and other urban settlements live in slums. Their homes are built of substandard materials, have tin or asbestos roofs and little ventilation, and are usually cramped for space.
The World Bank report says that while heat reduces productivity in existing work, it also discourages investments required for new jobs. Health burden and cooling have their own cost. For example, 90 percent of New Delhi’s street vendors reduced working hours due to heat in summer 2025, while 72 percent lost their stock of perishable food items to heat damage.
Power outages add to the crisis. When temperatures exceed 40 degrees Celsius, power outages in India increase by 20-50 percent, with the duration rising proportionally. Without action, cooling could account for 45 percent of India’s peak electricity load by 2050, up from 10 percent in 2016. This will not only put pressure on industrialization, but also leave workers with fewer chances to recover from the day’s stress.
The World Bank report pointed out that 120 million people in India, Bangladesh, and Nepal live in locations where outdoor heat stress already exceeds theoretical coping limits for at least one month annually. It highlighted a cost-benefit analysis, which found that heat early warning systems in Indian cities return roughly $50 for every $1 spent on them. Based on this, the report argued that authorities can protect residents and keep local economies working through the hottest months of the year by strengthening preparedness and response at the subnational level.
“In future decades, physiological and behavioral adaptation will undoubtedly help South Asians cope as heat stress levels rise. But the pace and scale of projected warming will increasingly test the limits of individual adaptation,” said the World Bank report.
Recently, the Indian government added heat waves to the list of natural calamities. This can help the government access funds for sustainable development goals (SDG). A policy framework for providing relief assistance through state and federal disaster response fund is being prepared, the government told Parliament in August. Heat Wave Mitigation Projects are now eligible under the Disaster Mitigation Funds, it added.
Rights activists, however, point out a crucial gap — labor laws in South Asian countries neither set any temperature threshold for safe work nor recognize heatstroke or kidney disease as occupational illnesses worthy of compensation. The IIED report on Bangladesh calls for heat protection at work to become a binding legal requirement.
Such steps could prove useful for the entire South Asian workforce.

Millions of workers in India face a growing threat from extreme heat, but unlike floods or storms, heat often leaves no visible damage, only lost income. So what happens when rising temperatures make it impossible to work?
This report follows Shabnam, a tailor in Uttar Pradesh, and explores an unusual solution: insurance that pays workers automatically when temperatures cross a certain threshold.
Designed for informal workers who often lack financial safety nets, the scheme is already helping thousands in India cope with heat-related income losses.
But can a weather-triggered payout truly capture the realities of heat stress? From questions about fairness and affordability to the challenges of scaling heat wave insurance in a warming world, what can we learn from this bold experiment?

full_text:
The tropical city state known for superior transit has a tip or two for keeping transit manageable as cities heat up.
Shaded sidewalks, giant ceiling fans and minimal walking distances to transit stations. These are just a few of the secrets Singapore employs to keep its world-class transit system cool despite 100 degree tropical heat. The Cool Down recently posted a video by Not Just Bikes touring the city state's transportation system with a focus on cooling infrastructure.
"When humidity makes 30-degree-Celsius days feel closer to 40 (that's over 100 degrees Fahrenheit), getting around on foot can quickly become draining. But Singapore is offering a different model, showing how shade, fans, and smart transit design can make life in a hot city far more manageable," writes The Cool Down.
"Singapore's example suggests that heat adaptation is not just about adding more air conditioning. full_text:
Ranchi: The Ranchi office of the
India Meteorological Department (IMD) on Monday issued a red alert for extremely heavy rain in Chatra, Hazaribag, and Ramgarh districts from Tuesday to Wednesday under the influence of a weather system over northwest Bay of Bengal and adjoining areas. An orange alert was issued for Garhwa, Palamu, and Latehar while an yellow alert was issued for eight districts, including Ranchi.
The Met office also forecast thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds of 40-50 kmph at isolated places across the state on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Sunday’s well-marked low pressure area over northwest Bay of Bengal and adjoining West Bengal-north Odisha coasts moved nearly northwestwards and concentrated into a depression at 5.30 am on Monday over coastal West Bengal and adjoining areas of Bangladesh and northwest Bay of Bengal.
The system moved north-northwestwards at a speed of 6 kmph and lay centred around 30 km west-northwest of Kolkata, 70 km south-southeast of Bardhaman, 90 km west of Satkhira in Bangladesh, 140 km east-southeast of Bankura and 190 km northeast of Baleshwar at 11.30 am on Monday.
“It is very likely to move north-northwestwards and then northwestwards across Gangetic West Bengal, Jharkhand, and Bihar during the next 24 hours,” head of Ranchi office, Baburaj PP said.
“Light to moderate rainfall at most places with heavy to very heavy rainfall at a few places is very likely on August 17, heavy to very heavy rainfall at a few places and extremely heavy rainfall at isolated places on August 18, heavy rainfall at isolated places on August 19,” he said.
Light to moderate rainfall with thunderstorms occurred at a few places, while heavy rainfall was recorded at isolated places on Monday. The highest rainfall, 90.8 mm, was recorded at Dhalbhumgarh in East Singhbhum. The highest maximum temperature, 34.6°C, was recorded at Baharagora, and the lowest minimum temperature, 21.6°C, at Latehar.

An Extreme Heat Warning returns to the Big Bend today from 11 a.m. until 8 p.m.
Leon County has activated its extreme heat response, and every library location will be open today as a cooling station. All six branch libraries, which are normally closed on Mondays, will be open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.
Cooling stations offer water, restrooms, activities and air-conditioned space for anyone seeking relief from the heat.
The main library on Park Avenue will be open for its regular Monday hours and is also available for cooling.
Here's the Leon County news release:
The National Weather Service has issued an Extreme Heat Warning for Leon County, in effect Monday, Aug. 17, from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., with heat index values up to 115 degrees expected.
In response, Leon County has activated its extreme heat response, and every County library location will be open Monday as a cooling station. All six branch libraries, which are normally closed on Mondays, will be open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.
Cooling stations offer water, restrooms, activities and indoor, air-conditioned space for anyone seeking relief from the heat. The LeRoy Collins Leon County Main Library will be open its regular Monday hours, 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. Residents who need relief today can visit the Main Library, open until 6 p.m. Sunday.
Cooling station locations for Monday, Aug. 17
• LeRoy Collins Leon County Main Library, 200 W. Park Ave. (10 a.m. to 9 p.m.)
• Bruce J. Host Northeast Branch Library, 5513 Thomasville Road (10 a.m. to 6 p.m.)
• Dr. B.L. Perry Jr. Branch Library, 2817 S. Adams St. (10 a.m. to 6 p.m.)
• Eastside Branch Library, 1583 Pedrick Road (10 a.m. to 6 p.m.)
• Jane G. Sauls Fort Braden Branch Library, 16327 Blountstown Highway (10 a.m. to 6 p.m.)
• Lake Jackson Branch Library, 3840-300 N. Monroe St. (10 a.m. to 6 p.m.)
• Woodville Branch Library, 8000 Old Woodville Road (10 a.m. to 6 p.m.)
"Leon County prepares for extreme weather in all its forms, and that includes heat," said Leon County Commission Chairman Christian Caban.
"County Emergency Management teams are focused on the forecast and responding now. I want to thank the first responders and County employees who will be working in these conditions to keep our community safe. Every County library will be open Monday as a cooling station, so please take care of yourself, check on your neighbors and use these facilities if you need relief."
How the County is protecting the community
• Vulnerable populations: Leon County Emergency Management is coordinating with the Big Bend Continuum of Care and community partners to address the needs of heat-vulnerable residents, including individuals experiencing homelessness, older adults living alone and households without reliable air conditioning.
• Medical readiness: Leon County Emergency Medical Services has increased staff readiness for a potential rise in heat-related calls.
• Animal safety: Leon County Animal Control is sharing information on heat risks to pets, including the need for hydration, shade and safe shelter.
• Outdoor workers and events: County departments are advising outdoor employees to follow heat safety protocols, and County Parks and Recreation and Tourism are advising event organizers at County facilities to take special care.
• Public information: The County is sharing heat safety updates through the Citizens Connect app, social media, the Emergency Information Portal and local media.
National Weather Service heat safety tips
• Drink plenty of water throughout the day, even if you do not feel thirsty. Avoid alcohol and caffeine.
• Stay in air-conditioned spaces as much as possible. If your home does not have air conditioning, visit a cooling station.
• Reduce, eliminate or reschedule strenuous outdoor activity to the coolest part of the day, typically early morning.
• Wear lightweight, loose-fitting, light-colored clothing.
• Never leave children, older adults or pets in a parked vehicle, even briefly. The inside of a car can reach deadly temperatures in minutes.
• Check on neighbors, friends and relatives, especially older adults, those with medical conditions and those without air conditioning.
• Know the signs of heat illness. Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness and nausea can signal heat exhaustion: move to a cool place, sip water and apply cool, wet cloths. A body temperature above 103 degrees, hot and dry skin, confusion or unconsciousness can signal heat stroke: call 911 immediately.
These measures remain in place until the National Weather Service warning expires. For the latest updates, visit the Leon County Emergency Information Portal at LeonCountyFL.gov/ei, download the Leon County Citizens Connect app or follow Leon County Government on social media.
